Examples

Source: vignettes/examples.Rmd
examples.Rmd

Two short worked examples. Both run on the package’s bundled earnings_panel (a synthetic, CPS-style two-wave panel of 7,600 women, 1982–2020; see ?earnings_panel) and aim to show the package’s two main modes — descriptive and causal — without doing a full analysis.

  • Example 1: Descriptive within/between decomposition
  • Example 2: Causal decomposition — the motherhood penalty
library(ineqx)
data("earnings_panel")

Example 1: Descriptive within/between decomposition

Women in earnings_panel are grouped into low/middle/high socioeconomic status (ses). We ask: how much earnings inequality lies within each SES tier vs between tiers, and how has that changed since 1982? For a clean annual cross-section we use each woman’s first wave (post == 0).

desc <- ineqx(
  y = "earnweek", ystat = "CV2",
  group = "ses",
  time = "year", ref = 1982,
  weights = "earnwt",
  data = subset(earnings_panel, post == 0)
)

We use ystat = "CV2" (squared coefficient of variation, σ2/μ2\sigma^2/\mu^2) rather than "Var" so that the high-income tier doesn’t mechanically dominate the decomposition. "VL" (variance of logs) is also accepted but is generally not recommended — see the FAQ.

print(desc)

Within- vs between-group inequality over time:

plot(desc, type = "wibe")

Decomposition of the change since 1982 into contributions from changing means (Δμ\Delta_\mu), changing dispersions (Δσ\Delta_\sigma), and changing group shares (Δπ\Delta_\pi):

plot(desc, type = "decomp")

CV2CV^2 rises from about 0.8 in 1982 to about 1.2 in 2019, and almost all of that inequality — and its growth — lies within SES tiers. The increase traces to growing within-group dispersion (Δσ\Delta_\sigma), partly offset by rising mean earnings (Δμ\Delta_\mu), which lower CV2CV^2 for a given standard deviation. Shifts in the SES composition (Δπ\Delta_\pi) play almost no role. This is the basic motivation for taking within-group inequality seriously.

Example 2: Causal decomposition — the motherhood penalty

Same dataset, now asking a causal question: how does motherhood affect earnings inequality among women, and how has that effect changed?

We restrict the sample to women with positive earnings and fit a difference-in-differences model (treatment = mother, post-period = post) with education-by-decade interactions for both the mean and log-SD of earnings. GAMLSS does the heavy lifting internally. For ystat = "CV2", keep the outcome in levels and use post for the DiD contrast; applying CV2 to first-differenced outcomes is not recommended.

df <- subset(earnings_panel, earnweek > 0)

causal <- ineqx(
  y = "earnweek", ystat = "CV2",
  treat = "mother", post = "post",
  group = "educ",
  time = "decade", ref = 1980,
  formula_mu    = ~ mother * post * educ * factor(decade) + age,
  formula_sigma = ~ mother * post * educ * factor(decade),
  weights = "earnwt",
  se = "delta",
  data = df
)
#> GAMLSS-RS iteration 1: Global Deviance = 397555473 
#> GAMLSS-RS iteration 2: Global Deviance = 397532171 
#> GAMLSS-RS iteration 3: Global Deviance = 397532169 
#> GAMLSS-RS iteration 4: Global Deviance = 397532169

Cross-sectional split: het and cov sub-components

The treatment effect on inequality at each time decomposes into τB=hetB+covB\tau_B = \text{het}_B + \text{cov}_B (between groups) and τW=hetW+covW\tau_W = \text{het}_W + \text{cov}_W (within groups). See the Model structure page for the exact formulas. plot(..., type = "wibe", stats = ...) shows all four series at once:

plot(causal, type = "wibe",
     stats = c("het_b", "cov_b", "het_w", "cov_w"),
     ci = TRUE)

The dominant series here is het_W — the within-group component driven by the average treatment effect on log-SD (λ‾\bar\lambda). It is positive and large: motherhood widens within-education earnings dispersion, though less so in later decades. The within-group cov_W term is negative and the between-group cov_B term (sorting of mean effects β\beta across education groups) is small and positive: the motherhood penalty is largest in the lowest-earning education group, which widens between-group gaps. Note this is exactly the kind of pattern that mean-based methods miss.

Longitudinal: behavioral / compositional / pre-treatment

How has the motherhood effect’s contribution to inequality changed since 1980? type = "shapley" displays the three-channel decomposition with the range across the six possible orderings:

plot(causal, type = "shapley")

The behavioral channel (Δβ+Δλ\Delta_\beta + \Delta_\lambda, how motherhood’s per-group effects have changed) is the largest and negative — the motherhood penalties on both the mean and the dispersion of earnings have shrunk since 1980, so motherhood adds less to inequality than it used to. The compositional channel (Δπ\Delta_\pi) is also negative: the share of women who become mothers has fallen. Pre-treatment shifts (Δμ+Δσ\Delta_\mu + \Delta_\sigma, changes in baseline inequality) push in the opposite direction: because baseline earnings have become more unequal, the same treatment effects now contribute more to inequality.

A more thorough analysis would add controls for race, marital status, and age splines; would model the pre-trends formally; and would use bootstrap rather than delta-method SEs. See ?ineqx, ?boot_config, and the Tutorial for the full toolbox.
